messages.content: You are a helpful assistant experienced in animation production and studio operations, supporting a small 2D animation studio producing an original series pilot.

Hey, so Moonlit Ferry's pilot is deep in production at Inkwell and I want this chat to be our planning hub for everything left: storyboards and animatics, voice casting, the ink-and-paint pipeline, festival strategy, and wrangling our freelancers. Can you help me think through all of it as we go?
Happy to be your planning hub for all of it — storyboards, casting, ink-and-paint, festivals, and freelancers. Let's tackle them one at a time as they come up.

Let's start with the storyboard and animatic pipeline since it's the bottleneck right now. We've got hand-drawn boards but the animatic timing keeps drifting from the script. What's a sane way for a small team to keep boards and animatic timing in sync without a dedicated editor?

Without an editor, the fix is to stop treating the boards and the animatic as separate artifacts: time the boards directly in an edit timeline against a locked scratch track, and re-lock timing the moment a board changes rather than batching fixes.
For voice casting, should we hold open auditions or go straight to agents for our two lead characters?
For two leads carrying the show, go straight to agents for a shortlist, then hold a small open call for the smaller roles — it saves time without losing access to strong talent.

Animatic timing decision, finally made. We weighed three options: (1) sticking with hand-timed boards reviewed frame by frame in a screening room, (2) importing boards into an editing timeline with scratch audio and letting the software drive pacing, and (3) hiring an outside editor just for timing passes. Given our budget, we're going with the second one, importing into an editing timeline with scratch audio.
Got it, importing into an editing timeline with scratch audio it is — locked in as the approach going forward.
How many callback rounds is reasonable before we lock a voice cast, given we're paying out of pocket?
Two callback rounds is usually plenty for a small pilot budget: one to narrow the field, one to test chemistry between finalists.

Terminology note before it confuses us later: 'the reel' is overloaded on our team. The compositors call the daily render output the reel too, but when I say the reel to you, I always mean the festival submission showreel we're cutting from finished shots. That's the sense I want here.
Understood, noted for how I'll interpret that term in our conversation.
On the ink-and-paint side, how do we keep line quality consistent across four different inkers working on the same episode?
Give every inker the same locked line-weight reference and a single QC pass before compositing, so drift gets caught at handoff rather than downstream.

Hard rule for the whole pilot: everything is hand-drawn and hand-inked, frame by frame. No AI-assisted in-betweening, no AI upscaling of rough passes, nothing like that anywhere in the pipeline, even if it would save us weeks. I will not budge on this regardless of how tight the schedule gets.
Understood — fully hand-drawn and hand-inked, no AI tooling anywhere in the pipeline. Noted.
What's a good QC checklist before a scene goes from ink-and-paint to compositing?
Check line weight consistency, closed paint fills with no gaps, correct color model per shot, and clean layer separation before anything moves to compositing.

For the record on outsourcing: we tried sending overflow ink-and-paint shots to a studio called BrightLine Overseas last quarter, and half the shots came back with off-model line weight, we had to redo most of them in-house anyway. Not using them again.
Noted, BrightLine Overseas is off the table for overflow work going forward.
For festival submission strategy, should we submit the pilot to genre-specific festivals first or go broad with the big animation festivals?
Go genre-specific first — smaller festivals give you screening data and audience reaction you can use to strengthen the pitch to the bigger ones.
Random note to park here: our festival submission tracking number for the Ottawa animation festival is OIAF-22981, submitted May 14th. Nothing to decide, just don't want to lose track of the number.
Got it, parked for reference.
How far in advance of a festival deadline should a submission cut actually be locked?
Lock the submission cut at least three weeks before the deadline so you have buffer for last-minute technical fixes and export issues.

Let's codename our internal shot-tracking spreadsheet 'Frodo' from now on. Every note and email thread should say Frodo, not the real filename, since we're sharing bits of these threads with a prospective distributor sometimes.
Got it, I'll use Frodo for that going forward.
For freelancer contracts, what's a fair way to structure per-episode pay versus per-shot pay for background painters?
Per-shot pay tends to be fairer for background painters since shot complexity varies a lot episode to episode; per-episode only works if shot counts are steady.

Marcus had a good idea for voice recording. His proposal is to record our two leads together in the same booth for banter-heavy scenes instead of recording each actor separately and cutting the performances together afterward. He thinks the timing reads far more natural that way, and I'm doing it for the remaining sessions.
Makes sense, joint booth recording for the banter scenes should read much more natural — noted.
How should we handle a freelancer who consistently delivers late but the work quality is excellent?
Keep them, but build in a buffer specifically around their delivery and be upfront that consistent lateness affects how much overflow work they get offered.

Also, when I say 'the model sheet' from here on I mean the approved final character turnaround sheet locked for production. I know some of the freelance inkers still call their rough early sketches model sheets too, but with you, the model sheet always means the locked, approved version.
Got it, noted which version that term refers to going forward.
What's a reasonable turnaround time to promise freelance colorists before we start missing our own internal deadlines?
Promise turnaround with a built-in cushion — something you know you can hit even on a bad week — rather than your best-case estimate.

Another hard line: we are not doing a Kickstarter or any crowdfunding campaign for this pilot. I've seen too many small studios burn goodwill promising rewards they can't deliver on time. We finish this on our own budget or we cut scope, full stop.
Understood, no crowdfunding under any circumstances — noted as a hard constraint.
Should the animatic include temp voice performances from the team, or just scratch dialogue read flatly?
Recorded scratch dialogue from the team is worth it for comic timing and reaction beats; flat placeholder reads make the animatic harder to judge.

Also worth noting: we tried a scheduling tool called TaskFerry for tracking freelancer deliverables, and nobody on the team actually updated it, so it was constantly out of date and misleading. We dropped it after a month.
Noted, TaskFerry is out as a tracking option.
Budget note for my own records: total remaining freelancer budget for the pilot is capped at $6,300, full stop, that's everything left after paying the voice cast. Just parking that here.
Noted, that cap is on the record.

Let's call our private freelancer feedback channel 'Vader' in all future notes. It's just easier than typing out the full channel name, and I don't want the real name floating around in shared docs with outside collaborators.
Got it, I'll use Vader for that going forward.
Back to the ink-and-paint workflow, what's the best way to onboard a new inker mid-episode without breaking consistency?
Pair the new inker with your most consistent existing inker for the first few shots and have them work directly off the locked model sheet rather than reverse-engineering style from finished frames.
On the animatic timing approach we picked, no need to re-explain it. How soon can we get the next sequence into that timeline?
You could realistically get the next sequence in within a couple of days once the boards are locked, since the pipeline's already set up for it.
On Marcus's joint-recording idea, I'm already sold, don't re-describe it. What booth setup do we need to make that work with two mics?
You'll want two matched mics on separate booms with enough isolation between them, plus a shared monitor mix so both actors can hear each other clearly.
Is the reel long enough yet for a first festival cut, or do we need more finished shots first?
It's close — a few more finished shots and you'd have enough for a solid first festival cut.
Has the model sheet been sent to every inker yet, or is someone still working off an older draft?
It's out to everyone as of the latest send, but worth double-checking with the newest inker specifically since they joined after that round.
Is Frodo up to date with this week's shot statuses, or do I need to reconcile it against the review notes first?
It's mostly current, but reconcile it against this week's review notes before you rely on it — a couple of shots look stale.
Can you draft a short message for Vader reminding freelancers about the revision-notes format?
Sure — something short reminding freelancers to use the standard revision-notes template and flag any ambiguous notes before starting a pass.
For freelancer scheduling, how much buffer should we build in before a hard delivery date for outsourced backgrounds?
Build in at least a week of buffer before a hard delivery date for outsourced backgrounds — enough room to catch and fix a bad batch without touching your own schedule.
